rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse targets people who enjoy worldly things and passions while seeking a reputation for sincerity and piety they lack.
rows.anchor: Those who exult in what they have brought about while wanting to be praised for what they have not done

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators identify several forms of hypocrisy and deceit as possible targets of the verse.
rows.anchor: The commentators mention different kinds of hypocrisy and deceit to which this verse seems to be referring.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: One reported occasion is hypocrites excusing themselves from the Prophet's battle expedition, then seeking pardon and praise on his return.
rows.anchor: It is reported by some that this verse was revealed in connection with certain hypocrites who would find an excuse not to go out with the Prophet

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the target as hypocrites generally, who sought praise for faith they did not possess.
rows.anchor: Or it refers simply to the hypocrites in general, those who wanted to be praised for a faith they did not possess.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others connect the verse to People of the Book distorting scripture while wanting recognition as devout religious people.
rows.anchor: Others say it refers to the practices of People of the Book, such as distorting their scriptures and then wanting to be praised as devoted people of religion.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: A further reading links it to concealing the truth in 3:187 while seeking praise as learned.
rows.anchor: Or it refers to the concealing of truth mentioned in v. 187, exulting in this concealment while still desiring to be praised as learned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The single-soul creation is also cited at 6:98, 7:189, 31:28, and 39:6; creation of its mate is also cited at 7:189 and 39:6.
rows.anchor: That God created human beings from a single soul is also mentioned in 6:98; 7:189; 31:28; 39:6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses present making human mates as a divine gift for which humanity should be grateful and stand in awe.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere, God’s having made for human beings “mates from among themselves” or “in pairs” is considered a Divine gift

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse moves from singularity, reflecting God's oneness, to duality and then the multiplicity of humanity.
rows.anchor: The present verse indicates a progression in human creation from singularity

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The single soul is widely identified as Adam and its mate as Eve (Ḥawwāʾ).
rows.anchor: The single soul is widely understood to refer to Adam, and its mate to Eve (Ḥawwāʾ).

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Although nafs is grammatically feminine and zawj masculine, this grammatical mismatch does not trouble the Adam-and-Eve identification for most commentators.
rows.anchor: does not necessarily make the correlation to Adam and Eve, respectively, problematic for most commentators

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interwoven masculine and feminine references suggest reciprocity between the sexes in human relations and marriage, also implied at 2:187 and 30:21.
rows.anchor: The interweaving of masculine and feminine references suggests a reciprocity of the masculine and feminine in human relations and marriage

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators typically connect the verse with Eve's creation from Adam's rib as recounted in Genesis 2:21–23.
rows.anchor: Commentators typically understand this verse as a reference to the story of Eve’s creation from Adam’s rib as found in Genesis 2:21–23

rows.speaker: some modern commentators
rows.claim: Some modern commentators are skeptical of the rib association because it relies too heavily on Biblical tradition.
rows.anchor: although some modern commentators are skeptical of this association, feeling it relies too heavily on the Biblical tradition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Canonical hadith references Eve's creation from Adam's rib, but the Quran never explicitly recounts Eve's creation.
rows.anchor: The story of Eve’s creation from Adam’s rib is referenced in the canonical Ḥadīth, but the Quran nowhere explicitly recounts Eve’s creation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Minhā may mean Eve was made of the same nature as Adam; min anfus can mean of the same type or character, as at 3:164, 9:128, and 16:72.
rows.anchor: the mate (Eve) was created of the same nature as the original

rows.speaker: Muḥammad al-Bāqir
rows.claim: The fifth Shiite Imam reportedly said Eve was created from the same superior clay as Adam.
rows.anchor: The fifth Shiite Imam, Muhammad al-Bāqir (d. ca. 114/732), reportedly said that Eve was created from the same superior clay as Adam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Common parentage is meant to encourage love among all people and discourage boasting about ancestry.
rows.anchor: The statement regarding humanity’s common origin from a single soul and its mate could also be meant to engender brotherly and sisterly love between all human beings

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The wording about invoking God and family relations may allude to the pre-Islamic Arab practice of swearing by both.
rows.anchor: Reverence God, through Whom you demand your rights of one another, and family relations may be related to the pre-Islamic Arab practice of swearing upon “God and family relations.”

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most favor reading the passage as commanding obedience to God and good relations with one's family.
rows.anchor: However, most favor the view that this passage instructs men to reverence God through obedience to His commands and to reverence family relations by maintaining good relations with family members.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arḥām means family relations; its singular raḥim primarily means womb and shares a root with mercy and the Divine Name al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: Family relations translates arḥām; the singular is raḥim, the primary meaning of which is “womb,” derived from the same root as raḥmah

rows.speaker: a ḥadīth
rows.claim: A hadith says the Compassionate created the womb, maintaining its ties earns God's ties, and severing them brings God's severance.
rows.anchor:
A ḥadīth states, “The
Compassionate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages pair worship of God with commands to treat family well.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere, the imperative to worship God is paired with commands to be good to family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's first part establishes kinship among all humanity and its latter part commands care for relatives, together making responsibility to all people a divine imperative.
rows.anchor: The first part of this verse indicates the kinship of all human beings, as they are created from the same soul and mate, while the latter part commands reverence for one’s relatives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Besides fathers' wives in 4:22, Muslim men cannot marry mothers, daughters, or sisters; mothers and daughters include grandmothers and granddaughters, and sisters include full and half siblings.
rows.anchor: Muslim men cannot marry their mothers, including grandmothers; their daughters, including granddaughters; or their sisters, including both full and half siblings

rows.speaker: al-Shāfiʿī
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī suggests a biological daughter born out of wedlock might not be covered by the marriage prohibition.
rows.anchor:
Al-
Shāfiʿī suggests that a man’s biological daughter born out of wedlock might not be subject to this prohibition

rows.speaker: all other schools of law
rows.claim: All other legal schools prohibit marrying any biological daughter, including one born out of wedlock.
rows.anchor: but all other schools of law prohibit marriage to any biological daughter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A milk-mother is a nonbiological woman who nurses a child; parents may pay a wet nurse under 2:233 and 65:6.
rows.anchor: A milk-mother is a wet nurse, a woman who nurses a child, but who is not the child’s biological mother.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk-siblings are otherwise unrelated children nursed by the same woman, and suckling creates a legal status like blood relations.
rows.anchor:
Milk-siblings (here milk-sisters
) are otherwise unrelated persons who, as infants or children, were wet-nursed by the same woman.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A woman who nursed a man is his maḥram, requiring no covering before her and prohibiting marriage; these rules also apply to her husband's and her biological children and others she nursed.
rows.anchor: meaning that she does not need to cover in front of him and he can never marry her.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man may marry the sister of his milk-son or the mother of his milk-brother as exceptions to the suckling rules.
rows.anchor: Two exceptions are that a man can marry the sister of his milk-son or the mother of his milk-brother

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah maintained that a revealed verse set ten sucklings for establishing milk relations, later changed to five.
rows.anchor: ʿĀʾishah maintained that a verse had been revealed requiring ten sucklings for the establishment of milk relations, but this was later changed to five

rows.speaker: a more widely transmitted report
rows.claim: A report says one or two sucklings do not establish legal milk relations, leading some to require at least three.
rows.anchor: A more widely transmitted report states that “one or two sucklings” do not establish legal milk relations, which led some to claim that at least three sucklings were required.

rows.speaker: al-Shāfiʿī
rows.claim: On the basis of other hadiths, al-Shāfiʿī required at least five sucklings.
rows.anchor: on the basis of other aḥādīth, al-Shāfiʿī required that a child be suckled at least five times

rows.speaker: Twelver Shiite school
rows.claim: The Twelver Shiite school requires fifteen sucklings, with variants requiring ten.
rows.anchor: the Twelver Shiite school requires fifteen (or, variously, ten;Ṭs).

rows.speaker: most legal scholars
rows.claim: Most legal scholars require nursing to occur in the child's first two to three years.
rows.anchor: For most legal scholars, the nursing has to occur within the first two to three years of the child’s life

rows.speaker: community consensus
rows.claim: The community's consensus is that the exception for unconsummated marriage clearly applies only to stepdaughters, not their mothers.
rows.anchor: The consensus of the community is that the exception only clearly applied to stepdaughters

rows.speaker: some early authorities
rows.claim: Some early authorities reportedly held that a man's wife's mother is prohibited only after he consummates marriage with the wife.
rows.anchor: some early authorities reportedly held that only when one had consummated marriage with a woman was one prohibited from marrying her mother

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some reportedly read an addition limiting the prohibition on wives' mothers to those whose marriage was consummated.
rows.anchor: Some reportedly read the verse with the following addition: and the mothers of your wives “with whom you have consummated marriage”

rows.speaker: early scholars
rows.claim: As in the discussion of 4:21, early scholars disputed which intimate contact legally constituted consummation.
rows.anchor: As in the discussion of v. 21, some early scholars debated the extent of intimate contact that legally constituted consummation

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some held that any intimate contact with a woman prohibited marriage to her daughter.
rows.anchor: Some viewed any intimate contact with a woman as prohibiting marriage to her daughter

rows.speaker: Shāfiʿī school
rows.claim: The Shāfiʿī school held that this prohibition applies only in the case of marriage.
rows.anchor: the Shāfiʿī school held that the prohibition pertained only in the case of marriage

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some derive rabībah and rabīb from a stepparent undertaking stepchildren's upbringing, an idea reinforced by “in your care.”
rows.anchor: The terms rabībah for “stepdaughter” and rabīb for “stepson” are said by some commentators to derive from the fact that a stepparent often undertakes the raising

rows.speaker: a minority tradition
rows.claim: A minority tradition treats being in the stepfather's care as a condition and says stepdaughters outside his home remain marriageable.
rows.anchor: A minority tradition suggests that this means that stepdaughters not living with their stepfathers are potential marriage partners.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most regard “in your care” as descriptive, not a legal condition; ordinary close family contact is what makes stepchildren forbidden spouses.
rows.anchor: But most understand this not as a condition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on marrying sons' former wives applies whether or not the marriage was consummated.
rows.anchor: the prohibition against marrying former wives of one’s sons applies regardless of whether the marriage was consummated or not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sons-from-loins limitation includes wives of milk-sons but excludes adoptive sons.
rows.anchor: The prohibition is limited to the wives of your sons who are from your loins, which includes the wives of one’s milk-sons

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators connect the rule to the Prophet's marriage to Zayd ibn Ḥārithah's former wife; because Zayd was adopted, not from his loins, the marriage was permissible.
rows.anchor: Some commentators connected this verse to the Prophet’s marrying the former wife of his adopted son, Zayd ibn Ḥārithah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marrying two sisters together is prohibited, while marriages arranged before revelation could stand.
rows.anchor: Marrying two sisters is forbidden, save for what is past, meaning that such marriages arranged prior to the revelation of this verse could stand

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly told converts who had two wives who were sisters to divorce one.
rows.anchor: the Prophet reportedly ordered men who desired to enter Islam, but had two sister wives, to divorce one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uqtulū anfusakum can mean slay yourselves or metaphorically mortify yourselves by killing vain desires, as in 2:54's command to Israelites after the golden calf.
rows.anchor: Lay down your lives translates uqtulū anfusakum, which could also be rendered “slay yourselves” or, metaphorically, “mortify yourselves”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the verse as addressing Jews and invoking 2:54 to suggest few contemporaries would obey such a command.
rows.anchor: Some see the present verse as addressing the Jews and as referencing the command in 2:54

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to leave home tested earlier prophets and their communities as well as Muhammad.
rows.anchor: The verse suggests that they would also have been unwilling to follow a Divine command to leave your homes, a command that tested many earlier prophets and prophetic communities, as well as Muhammad’s.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan followers' migration to Madinah earned them the status of Emigrants; before Makkah's conquest, hijrah there was required for full Muslim community membership.
rows.anchor: It was, in part, the willingness of the Prophet’s Makkan followers to leave their homes and families and migrate to Madinah that earned them the high religious status of “Emigrants”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some see the verse as continuing to address the two men in 4:60–65 who sought judgment from someone other than the Prophet.
rows.anchor:
Some see the present verse as continuing to address specifically the two men
who sought judgment from someone other than the Prophet referenced in vv.60–65

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it may address all whose belief claims were doubtful, including certain Jews, Madinan hypocrites, or others.
rows.anchor: although it may speak in general to all those whose claims of belief were questionable, whether they were certain Jews, Madinan hypocrites, or others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doing what they were told likely means consulting God and the Prophet in their affairs as commanded at 4:59; this would benefit them in both worlds and strengthen their faith.
rows.anchor: Had they done as they were told (which, in context, likely means to consult God and the Prophet in their affairs; see v. 59), it would have been better for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obedience would better convince others of sincerity and give them greater firmness, since hypocrites are always weak in resolve.
rows.anchor: It would have better convinced others of their sincerity and given them greater resolution in their own beliefs and actions, since the resolution of the hypocrite is always weak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The great reward from God's Presence, also mentioned at 4:40, is understood as a spiritual reward beyond physical delight, sometimes linked to seeing God or being overwhelmed by love and knowledge of Him.
rows.anchor: has been understood as a spiritual reward received from God’s very Presence that surpasses any physical reward or delight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the straight path, the commentary directs readers to 1:6.
rows.anchor: For straight path, see 1:6c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage is linked to 4:59; the obedient share the blessed people's guidance and success in this life and Paradise in the next.
rows.anchor: Cf. 4:59 and commentary. Those who are obedient are among those whom God has blessed, that is, those who have been granted guidance and success in this life and Paradise in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The obedient will enjoy the company of the finest people in Paradise, including prophets.
rows.anchor: Moreover, the verse indicates that they shall have the company of the most excellent in Paradise, including the prophets.

rows.speaker: some of the Prophet’s Companions
rows.claim: The verse was reportedly revealed when Companions feared that, since Muhammad would be exalted above them, they would lose his company in the Hereafter; it assures the obedient of his company after death.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed when some of the Prophet’s Companions expressed dismay at the thought that those who so enjoyed the Prophet’s company on earth would be denied it in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Several hadiths say the Prophet assured followers who love God, him, and the righteous that they will be with those they love in the next life despite shortcomings in deeds.
rows.anchor: According to several aḥādīth, the Prophet assured his followers that if they love God, the Prophet, and the righteous, although they may have fallen short in their own works

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: The truthful ones may mean those who sincerely believe and follow the prophets.
rows.anchor: are those who believe in and follow the prophets in complete sincerity (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the truthful ones as the most morally excellent among the prophets' companions.
rows.anchor: or the most morally excellent among their companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In later usage, ṣiddīq came to mean something like saint.
rows.anchor: in later usage, ṣiddīq came to denote something that approximates “saint.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Bakr received the epithet al-Ṣiddīq partly because he affirmed the Prophet's Night Journey when others doubted it and believed the first revelation.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s close Companion and the first Caliph, Abū Bakr, was given the epithet al-Ṣiddīq (the Truthful One)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Witnesses can also mean martyrs, sometimes glossed as those who die in God's way.
rows.anchor:
Witnesses (
shuhadāʾ) could also be rendered “martyrs” and is sometimes glossed as meaning those who die in the way of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting witnesses to religiously killed martyrs conflicts with Quranic uses for bearing covenant witness and testifying to truth in legal, religious, or spiritual matters.
rows.anchor: However, limiting witnesses to those killed for the sake of religion does not seem consistent with the wider Quranic usage

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says witnesses include all who testify to religious truth through argument or with sword and shield.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī argues that the word refers to all who bear witness to the truth of religion, whether they do so by proof and argument or with sword and shield

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: The righteous are those who do what is right publicly and privately.
rows.anchor: refers to those who do what is right both publicly and in secret (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage echoes 57:19, where the obedient are called truthful and witnesses, while here they accompany the truthful and witnesses.
rows.anchor: This passage echoes 57:19, where those who obey God and the Messenger are themselves described as

rows.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
rows.claim: In a Shiite report, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq identified the truthful and witnesses as the Imams and the righteous as their followers.
rows.anchor: According to a Shiite report, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq considered the truthful ones and the witnesses as references to the Imams

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads 4:68–69 as commentary on 1:6–7: those obeying God and the Prophet receive the prayed-for straight path and company of the blessed.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī sees vv. 68–69 as forming a commentary on 1:6–7

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses conclude the discussion of the People of the Book and imply that the Quran supplies irrefutable proof and clear light to reveal faithfulness to God's covenant and the truth about their prophets and revelations.
rows.anchor: the Quran has now brought them convincing proof
